mappings.rationale: Article 2 enumerates the additional lawful purposes (central processing, service/benefit to the data subject, scientific research) that permit an outbound transfer, which is the legal-authority-and-purpose determination in PRI-04.1/PRI-04 applied to the third-country transfer governed by DCH-25.

The publication and four-yearly re-evaluation of the adequacy list is a duty of SDAIA, not of a controller; the only organizational hook is the controller's obligation to identify this statutory requirement (CPL-01) and restrict outbound transfers to listed destinations (DCH-25).

Purely an internal administrative power of the competent authority to amend its own adequacy list and to negotiate with foreign supervisory authorities about de-listing — it imposes no obligation on any controller, so there is no SCF control and no ISO 27002 clause that corresponds.

The article grants the authority a suspension power; the only controller-side consequence is that transfers to a suspended destination must stop, which falls under DCH-25's restriction and governance of transfers to third countries.

Extending adequacy evaluation below national level to cities, special economic zones and global trade centers means a controller must know the sub-national geography where data actually resides, which is exactly DCH-19's inventory of geographic data location feeding the DCH-25 transfer decision.

The three named appropriate safeguards map one-to-one: "binding common rules" is PRI-01.5 Binding Corporate Rules, "standard contractual clauses" is PRI-07.1 data privacy requirements in contracts, and ISO 5.20/5.14 cover addressing information security in supplier agreements and rules for transferring information to external parties.

This is the chapeau establishing that exemption from Article 29(2)(b)/(c) does not exempt the transfer itself, which is DCH-25's core proposition that third-country transfers remain restricted and governed, with contractual safeguards (PRI-07.1) still required.

The requirement to embed standard personal-data-protection provisions into inter-governmental agreements and MOUs is literally the contract-requirements obligation in PRI-07.1 and TPM-05, and ISO 5.20 covers stating security requirements inside the agreement itself.

Non-recurring limited transfers require either standard contractual clauses (PRI-07.1) or a recipient holding a certificate from a licensed body, which is the independent third-party attestation model in TPM-05.8, with the sensitive-data carve-out governed by DCH-25.

Intra-group central-operations transfers requiring the controller and its affiliates to adopt binding common rules is a direct restatement of PRI-01.5 Binding Corporate Rules, with the SCC and licensed-certificate alternatives covered by PRI-07.1 and TPM-05.8.

Transfer to provide a service or benefit without violating the data subject's expectations is PRI-07's rule that PD is disclosed to third parties only for the notified purpose; the licensed-body certificate is TPM-05.8 and the sensitive-data prohibition is the special handling of sensitive PD categories in PRI-05.7.

The research exemption's binding constraint is that the transfer be limited to the minimum data required, which is PRI-04's minimization to the identified purpose, coupled with PRI-05.1 on limiting PD used for research and PRI-07.1 for the required contractual clauses.

Requiring safeguards to preserve the data subject's right to complain to the authority and seek compensation maps to PRI-06.4's process for handling data subject complaints, operating within the lawful-processing program of PRI-01 and enforced through the contractual safeguards of PRI-07.1.

The biennial review and amendment of the safeguard set is a regulator activity; the only controller obligation implied is CPL-01's ongoing identification and implementation of the currently applicable statutory and contractual requirements as they are amended.

Applying the Law to onward transfers by the foreign recipient is the flow-down of protection requirements to sub-recipients captured by TPM-05.2 and ISO 5.20, with the onward transfer itself remaining a governed third-country transfer under DCH-25.

Loss of the exemption is triggered by the controller failing to implement safeguards or the authority judging them inadequate — a determination of non-compliance with a statutory obligation, which is CPL-01.1's documented review of non-compliance instances driving remediation.

The dual duty to stop the transfer and notify the foreign recipients matches PRI-03.10's cessation of sharing PD and PRI-07.3's obligation to inform third parties of a change affecting PD already shared with them.

Article 7(1) mandates a pre-transfer privacy risk assessment and names the two triggering cases, which is precisely RSK-10's Data Protection Impact Assessment combined with RSK-04.3's definition of the instances that compel a risk assessment.

The six prescribed assessment elements (legal basis, nature and geographic scope, safeguard adequacy, data minimization, material/moral impact and likelihood, mitigating controls) are the required content of a DPIA under RSK-10 executed via the methodology of RSK-04.2, with element (D) being PRI-04 minimization.
An undertaking by SDAIA to publish supplementary guides and guidelines — it creates no obligation, process or evidence for a controller, so there is nothing in SCF or ISO 27002 to map it to.
A commencement clause fixing entry into force on publication in the Official Gazette; it is a legal effectivity provision with no control content whatsoever.
